drug_class: Retinoid (a type of vitamin A-related cancer medicine)
purpose: Bexarotene is used to treat a type of skin cancer called cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL), which causes scaly, rash-like patches or tumors on the skin. It is used when other treatments have not worked well enough. It comes as both a capsule you swallow and a gel you apply directly to the skin.
how_it_works: Bexarotene belongs to a family of medicines related to vitamin A. It works by attaching to special proteins inside cancer cells called retinoid X receptors, which then tell the abnormal cells to stop growing and eventually die. Think of it like flipping a switch inside the cancer cells that slows down the disease.
common_side_effects: Very high levels of fats (triglycerides and cholesterol) in your blood, low thyroid hormone levels (which can cause tiredness and weight gain), dry skin, headache, nausea, muscle weakness, sensitivity to sunlight, and swelling in your legs or feet. Lab blood tests will be done regularly to monitor these effects.
warnings: Bexarotene can cause very high triglyceride levels, which can be dangerous and may require additional medication. It can seriously harm an unborn baby, so women must not become pregnant while taking it and must use two reliable forms of birth control. It can lower your white blood cell count, making infections more likely. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and use sunscreen, as this medicine increases your sensitivity to sunlight. Do not take vitamin A supplements while on this medication.
typical_dosing: The capsule dose is usually 300 mg per square meter of your body surface area, taken once daily with a meal. Your doctor will calculate the exact dose based on your height and weight. The gel is applied once every other day at first and gradually increased up to 4 times daily, depending on how well you tolerate it. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
